# Exact failure of the central-symmetry plus endpoint-centroid scalar certificate

This concerns a proposed sufficient certificate, not the actual depth
conjecture. The displayed volume triples are realizable by compatible
centrally symmetric fibers, and those particular realizations have a
strictly better actual middle-point bound.

## 1. The two certificates and their envelope

Normalize the larger endpoint volume to one, let (0<a\le1), and set

\[
\Gamma=\left(\frac d{d+1}\right)^d,
\qquad v=2^{-d}(1+a^{1/d})^d,
\qquad k\ge v.
\]

The proposed pair of lower bounds is

\[
B_0=\frac k2+a\max\left\{0,1-\frac{k}{2v}\right\},
\qquad B_1=\Gamma.
\tag{1}
\]

Indeed a centrally symmetric middle body has raw ordinary depth (k/2)
at its symmetry center. A dominated midpoint measure of mass (a)
and density at most (a/v) puts at least

\(a-(a/v)(k/2)\)

in each through-center cap when this expression is positive. Its
injection into the two endpoint cuts gives (B_0). The larger endpoint
centroid gives (B_1). Thus these are legitimate lower certificates;
the question is whether they suffice numerically for all volumes.

Their doubled maximum is

\[
2\max(B_0,B_1)
 =\max\{2\Gamma,k,2a+(1-a/v)k\}.
\tag{2}
\]

The proposed assertion would require (2) to be at least
\(\Gamma(k+a+1)\). It is false already in dimension one, and also in
dimension two.

## 2. A rational interval counterexample to the certificate

Take

\[
d=1,\quad a=\frac14,\quad v=\frac58,\quad
k=\frac56,\quad \Gamma=\frac12.
\]

Then (v<k<2v), and

\[
B_0=\frac5{12}+\frac14\left(1-\frac23\right)=\frac12=B_1.
\]

The required raw target is

\[
\frac\Gamma2(k+a+1)=\frac14\frac{25}{12}=\frac{25}{48},
\]

which exceeds both certificates by (1/48).

In fact this occurs throughout an exact open interval. For (0<a<1/3),
let

\[
v=\frac{1+a}{2},\qquad
k=\frac{(1-2a)(1+a)}{1-a}.
\]

Direct subtraction gives

\[
k-v=\frac{(1+a)(1-3a)}{2(1-a)}>0,
\quad 2v-k=\frac{a(1+a)}{1-a}>0,
\quad k-(1-a)=\frac{a(1-3a)}{1-a}>0.
\]

The first two identities put the middle certificate in its affine
branch, where (B_0=B_1=1/2). The last identity makes the requested
target strictly greater than (1/2).

## 3. An exact planar counterexample and its open failure interval

Take

\[
d=2,\quad a=\frac4{25},\quad v=\frac{49}{100},\quad
\Gamma=\frac49,\quad k=\frac{6272}{7425}.
\]

Since (1-a/v=33/49), the chosen (k) satisfies

\[
k=\frac{2(\Gamma-a)}{1-a/v}.
\]

It lies strictly between (v) and (2v). Therefore (B_0=B_1=4/9).
The original total volume and the exact certificate gap are

\[
k+a+1=\frac{14885}{7425},
\qquad
\frac\Gamma2(k+a+1)-\frac49=\frac{14}{13365}>0.
\tag{3}
\]

For the full failure interval, write (a=x^2), (v=(1+x)^2/4), and
retain (k=2(\Gamma-a)/(1-a/v)). The normalization denominator is
positive for (0<x<1). At the lower target crossing (k=1-a), the
relevant scalar expression factors exactly as

\[
\begin{aligned}
4\left[v(1+a-2\Gamma)-a(1-a)\right]
 &=(1+x)^2(1+x^2-8/9)-4x^2(1-x^2)\\
 &=\frac{(x+1)(3x-1)(15x^2-4x-1)}9.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]

It is negative precisely on the displayed positive interval

\[
\frac13<x<\frac{2+\sqrt{19}}{15}.
\tag{5}
\]

On (5), (x<1/2), so (v+a<13/16<8/9=2\Gamma). This gives

\(k>v\).

Also (v>\Gamma), which gives (k<2v). Finally (4) gives

\[
k-(1-a)
 =-\frac{v(1+a-2\Gamma)-a(1-a)}{v-a}>0.
\]

Thus throughout (5), both certificates equal (\Gamma) and the target
strictly exceeds (\Gamma).

## 4. Actual realizability, and why this is not a depth counterexample

Both rational examples are geometrically realizable. More generally let
\(B=[-1/2,1/2]^d\), let (A=a^{1/d}B\), and let (K=k^{1/d}B\).
All three are centrally symmetric about zero, with the stated volumes.
Their midpoint is

\[
(A+B)/2=\frac{1+a^{1/d}}2 B,
\]

of volume (v\), and is contained in (K) because (k\ge v).
The convex hull of the layers at integer bases (-1,0,1) therefore
has exactly the indicated three fibers, all with positive volume.

However the actual point (Y=(0,0)) has raw mixed depth at least

\[
\frac k2+a.
\tag{6}
\]

For a nonvertical halfspace through (Y), the middle contribution is
exactly (k/2). The reflected copy (-A=A\) is contained in (B).
Every point of the negative-base (A) fiber is either captured, or its
reflection in the positive-base copy is captured. This gives endpoint
capture at least (a), including equality boundaries, which have zero

(d)-volume for a nonzero continuous normal. A pure integer halfspace
through (Y) captures the whole middle fiber and at least one endpoint,
so its mass is at least (k+a). A halfspace merely containing (Y) can
be shrunk to one through it without increasing mass.

For the interval example, (6) equals (2/3>25/48). For the planar
example it exceeds the target by

\[
\frac k2+a-\frac29(k+a+1)=\frac{9146}{66825}>0.
\]

Consequently these examples disprove only the claim that the two
coarse bounds (1), by themselves, cover every admissible volume triple.
They do not disprove the desired mixed-integer inequality, or a stronger
argument retaining the actual coupling support or reflected endpoint
geometry.
